tldr: Magnette walks through every workflow and agentic pattern in LangChain4j's agentic modules with live demos, arguing you should start with plain workflows and add autonomy only when needed.
summary: After a refresher on LangChain4j AI services (system and user messages, @Tool classes, input and output guardrails with retry), Magnette defines an agent as a model working towards a goal with tools and context. In LangChain4j that is an interface annotated @Agent with a capability description and an output key, built with the agentic builder from the separate langchain4j-agentic dependency. Agents share state through the AgenticScope instead of passing messages, and a Planner interface (init, firstAction, nextAction) decides what runs next. All demos use dog-themed rescue scenarios on a local model via Ollama.

The first half covers workflows, which map onto ordinary control flow: sequence; loop with an exit-condition lambda on a reviewer's score, a max-iterations cap and an option to test the exit after every agent; parallel with your own executor and an output function to merge results; a parallel mapper that runs one agent per item of a collection; and conditional routing, where he recommends a classifier that returns an annotated enum rather than a string. Typed keys replace string output keys to catch typos and type mismatches at compile time. He adds human-in-the-loop agents for approval steps, optional agents and an error handler with attempt counting and retry, plain-Java non-AI agents, AgentListener hooks, the AgentMonitor's HTML report of topology and timing, and a lambda that picks a cheap or strong chat model per call.

After the break come the patterns in langchain4j-agentic-patterns. The LLM supervisor picks sub-agents itself, with an invocation cap and a choice of chat memory or summarised context; the smallest Llama 3.2 never delegated at all. The goal-oriented planner builds a graph from agents' inputs and outputs and follows the shortest path, fixed once chosen. Peer-to-peer fires any agent whose inputs changed; blackboard adds a conflict strategy choosing who goes next. Voting aggregates verdicts (any 'not safe' vetoes ice skating), debate runs rounds through a shared debate context until a convergence strategy or round limit hands off to a judge, and Belief-Desire-Intention plans by prioritised desires with activation conditions and definitions of done.

He then implements a custom Planner in plain Java, nests loops, sequences, parallel mappers and voting planners (every pattern is itself an agent), and shows the declarative annotations (@SequenceAgent, @LoopAgent, @SupervisorAgent, @PlannerAgent), async agents, A2A integration and an agent registry. His advice: most client systems are workflows, so start there; the supervisor is the most flexible but costly and hard to audit. In the Q&A, Mario Fusco, who builds the agentic module, introduced a new router pattern backed by decision models that return probabilities instead of text, and invited contributions of new planners.
keyPoints: Agentic features need `langchain4j-agentic` for workflows and `langchain4j-agentic-patterns` for supervisor-free patterns such as GOAP, peer-to-peer, blackboard, voting, debate and BDI.
AgenticScope is the shared state between agents; the Planner interface with init, firstAction and nextAction drives every workflow and pattern.
Loops need an explicit exit condition plus a max-iteration cap; more iterations cost more tokens and do not fix poor inputs.
Use typed keys and enum outputs instead of strings for output keys and routing decisions to get compile-time safety.
AgentMonitor generates an HTML report with the agent topology and time spent per step, without needing Grafana.
A supervisor needs a capable model and has unpredictable paths and cost; the goal-oriented planner fixes a shortest path (fewest agents, not cheapest) from inputs and outputs.
Voters sharing the same model, tools or context share the same biases, so more voters do not guarantee independent judgements.
Workflows, patterns and non-AI agents are all agents and can be nested freely, so LangChain4j can even serve as a plain workflow orchestrator.
takeaways: Start new agentic features as sequence, loop, parallel or conditional workflows and move to autonomous patterns only when they fall short.
Replace string output keys with typed keys before your agent graph grows.
Put deterministic steps such as calculations in non-AI agents rather than asking an LLM.
Add a human-in-the-loop agent before any sensitive external action, and an error handler with bounded retries for flaky outputs like JSON.
Attach the AgentMonitor HTML report to see where an agentic system spends its time.

quotes.text: The patterns you don't use are the ones you don't need to debug.
Please don't write a planner that uses an LLM. That's not smart.

watchIf: You build LLM features in Java and need to choose how much control to give agents, with working LangChain4j code for each option.
